notes:
Registered endpoint: mean ambulance travel time to incidents in the zone during peak toll hours, relative to all other city ZIPs, 5 January to 31 August 2025 against 2023-24: -0.9% (-3.0 to +1.4), standard error 0.0113 on the log scale, 32 months. Composed prediction -1.8%; z_chain 0.66; z against the proportional alternative (-5.4%) 4.18; D_prop 17.0. The registered support condition is met: travel time did not fall in proportion to the rise in speed. z against no effect is -0.76 and the interval includes zero, so an improvement is not shown; the registration stated in advance that this test could not tell the chain from no effect. Whole post-period to September 2026 (secondary): -0.2% (-1.9 to +1.6). The within-zone control does not support a toll effect. In overnight hours, when the toll is a quarter of the peak toll, the zone's relative travel time fell more: -4.0% (-6.3 to -1.7) to August 2025 and -2.1% (-4.1 to -0.2) to September 2026. The triple difference (peak minus overnight) is +3.3% (+1.4 to +5.2), with a 2024 placebo of +0.2% (-1.6 to +2.0). Life-threatening incidents (initial severity 1 to 3): +5.2% (+2.6 to +7.9), but the 2024 placebo is +6.0% (+3.3 to +8.8), so the zone's relative travel time for these calls was already rising before the toll. Lower-priority incidents: -2.4% (-5.2 to +0.5). Total response time (call to arrival), all incidents: +0.8% (-4.5 to +6.5). Against Manhattan 60th-110th Street: +1.8% (-0.9 to +4.6) (2024 placebo +5.4% (+3.7 to +7.0)). Against downtown Brooklyn and Long Island City: +4.1% (+1.9 to +6.3) (placebo +5.5% (+1.6 to +9.5)). The 2024 placebo of the primary comparison is +1.6% (-0.8 to +4.0). Fire Incident Dispatch Data, same estimator: travel time -0.6% (-1.8 to +0.6) to August 2025 and +0.4% (-0.6 to +1.4) to September 2026. Levels: mean EMS travel time in the zone at peak hours was 558 s in 2023, 617 s in 2024, 661 s in 2025 and 712 s in January to September 2026; in the rest of the city 591, 647, 696 and 772 s. Travel time rose everywhere by about 7% a year, which is several times any effect of the toll. Lives (composition, not a test and not a result): the number of lives a year among cardiac arrests in the zone at peak hours depends on which measured change is used, and its sign is not determined. The registered peak estimate gives +0.3 (-0.7 to +2.0), the difference of peak and overnight hours gives -1.4 (-4.1 to -0.2), total response time gives -0.3 (-4.6 to +2.9), and no effect gives 0.0 (-1.4 to +1.3).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is changed from confirmed to unsettled under rule 8. The claim is a bridge with an endpoint test. Rule 8 measures discrimination against no effect: D = z_null^2 - z_chain^2 = 0.76^2 - 0.66^2 = 0.14, below 4. The registration computed D against a fall in proportion to speed (-5.4%), which gave 17.0, and named rules 1, 2 and 8 for the verdict. A registration cannot replace the D that rule 8 defines, so rule 8 applies as written and the endpoint's agreement with the composed prediction does not decide. The registration said in advance that the test could not tell the chain from no effect. Round 4 changed graph-triad-cold-asthma-absence in the same way (D = 3.0). The referee simulated the registered rule at the observed standard error: it returns confirmed with probability 0.80 if the toll had no effect, 0.87 if the chain is true, 0.50 if travel time rose by 1% and 0.01 if it fell in proportion to speed. Any estimate from -3.04% to +0.99% met the support condition. What the registered estimate shows is narrower than the first label: with calendar-month terms it excludes a fall in proportion to speed (z = 4.18). That exclusion does not survive a linear trend in the pre-period: the estimate is then -3.13% (-7.47 to +1.42) and z against the proportional fall is 1.03. The trend term was chosen after the data and decides nothing under rule 4. The registered estimator run at 17 false start dates in 2023-24 gives estimates from -0.2% to +4.9% with a standard deviation of 0.016 on the log scale, against the HAC standard error of 0.011, so the registered interval is too narrow. No improvement is shown: the interval includes zero and a rise of 1.4%. The overnight control argues against the toll as the cause of the peak estimate. In overnight hours, when the toll is a quarter of the peak toll, the zone's relative travel time fell by 4.0% (1.7 to 6.3), and peak minus overnight is +3.3% (+1.4 to +5.2), which is 4.0 combined standard errors from the composed prediction and 3.5 from zero. The overnight series is not stable before the toll either (false starts in 2023-24 give +4.4% to +12.1%), so it is not a clean control. Incidents in the zone fell by 3.0% relative to the rest of the city at peak (-4.3 to -1.7) and overnight (-5.4 to -0.5), which would free units at all hours. Link 2 is not stable: the registered exponent 0.317 is fitted mostly on the pandemic months; without March 2020 to June 2021 the slope is -0.62 (se 0.10), for 2022-24 it is -0.49 (se 0.12) and for 2023-24 it is -1.13 (se 0.40), which is a proportional response. The overnight ratio has nearly the same slope on taxi speed (-0.29, se 0.06) as the peak ratio, so the monthly co-movement is not specific to congested hours. The composed prediction is quoted as -1.68%, the median of the draws; the notes above give -1.8%, the mean of the log (-0.0178), and the z values use the mean. ZIP 10044 (Roosevelt Island) is in the zone list in analyses/congestion/common.py and is outside the toll zone; with the zone defined by dispatch areas M1 to M3, which exclude it, the peak estimate is -0.79% (-3.10 to +1.59). The script was fixed with the registration and is not corrected. Citywide, mean travel time rose from 559 s in 2023 to 607 s in 2024, 651 s in 2025 and 724 s in January to September 2026, and the share of incidents with no valid response time, which the analysis drops, rose from 4.4% to 6.3% in 2025 and 9.5% in 2026. The closure of Mount Sinai Beth Israel was registered as an alternative and has not been examined.
verdict_note: Unsettled under rule 8: the endpoint test cannot tell the composed chain from no effect (D = 0.14 against no effect; the registered rule returns confirmed with probability 0.80 if the toll did nothing). Peak ambulance travel time in the zone changed by -0.9% (-3.0 to +1.4) relative to the rest of the city, so no improvement is shown. A fall in proportion to the 5.7% rise in taxi speed is excluded by the registered estimate and not when a trend term is added. Overnight, when the toll is a quarter as large, the zone's relative travel time fell by 4.0%, which argues against the toll as the cause. The number of lives is not a result: between about -1.5 and +2 a year, sign not determined, depending on the comparison used.
lives_note: Not a result. Lives a year among cardiac arrests in the zone at peak hours, by the measured change used: registered peak estimate +0.3 (-0.7 to +2.0); peak minus overnight -1.4 (-4.1 to -0.2); total response time -0.3 (-4.6 to +2.9); composed prediction +0.7 (0.0 to +2.5). The count of 1,331 attended arrests includes the 43% pronounced dead on scene, the all-incident estimate is applied to calls whose own travel time rose by 5.2%, and odds ratios per minute are applied to about 3 seconds.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict changed from confirmed to unsettled under rule 8; the lives figure is no longer reported as a result; the script is not corrected (rule 9)
